title: Mood Lamp from a Recycled Jar

questions.q: In PWM, what does the 'duty cycle' control for an LED?
choices: The colour of the light
The brightness — the fraction of each fast cycle the pin stays on
The voltage, raising it above 3.3 V
How many LEDs are connected
questions.explain: A pin is only ever fully on or fully off, so brightness comes from the duty cycle: the proportion of each rapid cycle the pin spends on. A duty cycle of 0.5 keeps the LED on half the time, so it looks half as bright. gpiozero uses a 0–1 value per channel.

questions.q: Your RGB LED is wired as common-cathode (the default). When you ask for red, you get cyan, and vice versa. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
choices: The resistors are too large; use smaller ones
It is actually a common-anode LED; create it with active_high=False and connect the shared leg to 3.3 V
The GPIO pins are in the wrong numbering system; switch to physical pins
PWM is disabled; turn it on
questions.explain: Inverted colours are the classic sign of a common-anode LED being driven as if it were common-cathode. Setting active_high=False tells gpiozero the channels light when driven LOW, and the shared leg goes to 3.3 V instead of GND.

questions.q: Why does an RGB LED need three resistors instead of one shared resistor on the common leg?
choices: Three resistors make the colours brighter
Each colour is a separate LED that needs its own current limit; a shared resistor would let the brightness change as colours mix and would not protect each channel
gpiozero refuses to run with fewer than three resistors
The extra resistors store charge to smooth the fade
questions.explain: Each colour inside the package is a real LED with almost no resistance. One resistor per channel limits each colour's current independently; a single shared resistor would make the brightness of one colour depend on the others and would not protect each LED properly.

questions.q: What does the 'return' keyword do in a function like clamp(value)?
choices: It prints the value to the console
It hands a result back to whoever called the function, so it can be stored and used
It ends the whole program
It repeats the function from the start
questions.explain: return passes a value back out of the function to the caller. That is what lets you write half_red = dim((1,0,0), 0.5) and store the result, rather than the function just doing something with no usable answer.

questions.q: Why is a 'while True:' loop a good fit for a mood lamp?
choices: It runs the body exactly once and then stops
It runs its body over and over forever, so the lamp keeps glowing until you stop the program
It is the only loop that works with the random module
It automatically dims the LED to save power
questions.explain: while True never ends on its own because True is always true, so the body repeats indefinitely — perfect for a lamp that should keep fading colours until you press Stop. The random module then keeps each cycle unpredictable in lava mode.
